````markdown
# Phase B3a: real ports and the script-node runtime

**Date:** 2026-10-25 · **Branch:** `feature/modularize` · **Status:** built (fa05b121 to 37cc4b80, §8); B3b not yet
built, and the LSDj master-sync fix comes before it (§10).

Phase B of [modular-graph-design.md](modular-graph-design.md) moves the engine onto the graph in steps,
each held bit for bit to the B0 parity baseline ([modular-graph-phase-b0-design.md](modular-graph-phase-b0-design.md)).
B1 ran native on the executor, B2 ([modular-graph-phase-b2-design.md](modular-graph-phase-b2-design.md)) gave
the graph's structure to TS. B3, "the DSP kernel dissolves", is split in two: **B3a** (this document) makes the
kernel's input and output real wires and runs the kernel, unchanged, as one TS node in a new script-node
runtime; **B3b** splits that node into one protocol node per role and deletes the kernel. §10 records what
building B3a found.

## 0. Where B3a sits

Before B3a, `main` was merged into this branch (c2245f1b). Its one feature written against the old engine,
the physical-N8 cart mirror (`Engine::cartSystemId`), was ported onto the graph engine, and parity did not move:
the reliable link stays off for every parity ROM (each advertises caps `0xFF`), and no case reaches the empty
N8 FIFO read main changed. B3a starts from that merged tree, so its bar is the behaviour that ships.

Before B3a the kernel was a sealed box. `rp.dsp.kernel` was a native node with no ports, first in every plan
([B1 §3.3](modular-graph-phase-b1-design.md)). Its `process()` was `Engine::runKernelStage`: it handed the
staged host MIDI, the control-surface MIDI and last block's MI.OUT bytes to one `processBlock` call in a bare
QuickJS context (`DspRuntime`), then fanned six system-addressed sink kinds into the cores by id, in a fixed
order. Its structure (each system's role pipeline, the project stages) arrived separately, through
`dspSetSystems`, and the bundle through `compileScript` + `dspLoadKernel` at boot.

After B3a that I/O is wiring the planner can see: host I/O nodes, input ports on every system node, a
`serialOut` port on the Game Boy, and a kernel node whose settings are its structure, run by a script host every
Engine has. The sealed kernel, its fan-out and its three RPCs are gone (§5.4).

## 1. Decisions taken

| Question | Decision |
|---|---|
| Merge `main` before B3 or after? | **Before** (done: c2245f1b). B3 rewrites the code where NES MIDI reaches the N8 FIFO, which is where main had moved on. |
| How is B3 cut? | **B3a then B3b**, each with its own spec, plan and bit-identical check. B3a: the runtime and the ports, with the kernel as one script node. B3b: one protocol node per role, `kernelProjection` folded into `buildGraph`, zod out of the bundle, the kernel deleted. |
| Frame order on the new wires | **Sort at the source.** `rp.host.midi-in` stable-sorts the staged host MIDI by frame, so every queue keeps the ABI's frame-ordered promise (§3.4). |
| Kernel state across a structure change | **Reshape.** A script node may keep its instance across a settings change that alters its layout; the planner rebinds its ports by id and commits the new settings at the swap (§2.4). |
| Does an edit wait for the last edit's commit? | **Only when that commit's node reads its current settings to prepare.** A type that declares `RP_TYPE_STATELESS_PREPARE`, as every script type does, never holds `setGraph` back; its commits queue on the ring in push order (§2.4, §10). |
| How does one set of functions serve several types? | **The type-level calls take their type.** `descriptor`, `layout_for`, `query_memory` and `create` are handed the `rp_node_type` they are called through, which gains a `ctx` (§2.2, §10). |
| How does the bundle reach the engine? | **Embedded at build time**, as bytecode, and loaded when an Engine is constructed. No boot call (§2.5). |
| Host MIDI out's system tag | **Kept**, with its emission order, by a private 4-byte prefix on the kernel's one `midiOut` port that only `rp.host.midi-out` reads (§4.4). Transitional: B3b's nodes each have their own port. |
| The N8 cart mirror | **A node**, `rp.n8.cart-mirror`, wired by `buildGraph` from the first NES's kernel outputs (§3.5). TS's choice of cart system is the only one. |
| A throw in the kernel's JS | **The old rule**: the block's output up to the throw stands, the next block runs again; counted and logged once (§4.5). |
| Host block sizes | **Any, from 1 frame.** New parity groups pinned 1-frame blocks and FL-style ragged splits before B3a changed anything, and a bench measured per-call cost at tiny blocks while the old kernel still ran (§6, §7.4). |
| LSDj master sync in tiny blocks | **Pinned as it is, and fixed right after B3a**, as its own change, before B3b ports the decoder (§7.1, §10). |

## 2. The script-node runtime

### 2.1 One audio-side runtime per engine

`DspRuntime` became the **script host** ([ScriptHost.hpp](../packages/native/src/host/script/ScriptHost.hpp)): one
bare QuickJS runtime per `Engine` holding every script node instance, entered only by the thread that runs blocks
(the audio thread, or the caller's thread while quiescent), as the kernel's context was. Each Engine has its own: the
plugin's instances, the standalone, the SDL host, the CLI, the UI's `RenderHost` jobs and the Node addon never share
one.

A script node is reached through an ordinary `rp_node`: a native **shim** per instance that the planner creates,
activates and destroys like any node. The shim's `create` and `activate` run on the control thread and only allocate
the shim and its record. The JS instance behind it lives in the script host:

- **created** there by the first call the shim gets on the block thread, from the settings the shim was created
  with. In practice that is the `ports_changed` the planner sends every fresh instance when its plan is adopted, so
  the instance exists before that plan's first `process`; a `commit_settings` or `process` arriving first would
  create it too. An `activate` of a live instance (a new rate or block size) runs its JS hook at once only while
  quiescent, and otherwise just before its next `process`.
- **released** there once the plan that last held it is reclaimed: the shim's `destroy` (control thread) hands the
  record to the script host, which releases the JS instance at once while quiescent, and otherwise queues it on an
  SPSC ring (256 deep, with a control-side backlog behind it) that `beginBlock` drains at the top of the next block.
  The released record comes back on a second ring (512 deep) and `reclaim` deletes it on the control thread, so the
  audio thread frees nothing native. Closures that form cycles are freed at the audio runtime's next collection,
  inside a block.

So JS runs on one thread at a time, as it did. Creating an instance allocates in QuickJS on the block thread, as the
old `SetSystems` command, applied on the audio thread, did; so do parsing its settings there, the mask array
`portsChanged` receives and the frees of a release. They happen only at swaps and releases, which is accepted, though
a heavy `create` is an xrun source.

### 2.2 One control-side runtime for validation

The ABI's `layout_for` and `prepare_settings` run on the control thread, and a TS node's ports may be a function
of its settings (the kernel's are per system). The planner must keep validating a whole document before it
creates anything ([B1 §6](modular-graph-phase-b1-design.md)). So a second bare QuickJS runtime, created with
the Engine and loaded with the same bundle, answers those two calls for every script type: the definition's
`parseSettings` checks a settings object and its `layout` gives the ports, from the settings alone. It never holds an
instance and never runs `process`; the two runtimes share no JS values, only the bundle.

A bundle registers its definitions by appending them to the global `__rp_scriptNodes`
([register.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/script/register.ts)). Once it has run in both runtimes the host reads both
lists, requires each definition's id to match by index, and registers one `rp_node_type` per definition in one
package, `rp.script`, each declaring `RP_TYPE_STATELESS_PREPARE` (§2.4) and taking `reshapes` and `faultOnThrow` from
its definition. Every type is served by the same functions, which the ABI could not tell apart: its type-level calls
had no context (§10). So `descriptor`, `layout_for`, `query_memory` and `create` now take the `const rp_node_type*`
they are called through, and `rp_node_type` gains a trailing `ctx`, null for a C++ node and never read by the host,
which for a script type points at its definition's record ([rp_node.h](../packages/native/src/graph/rp_node.h)).

### 2.3 Marshalling

A node's `process` gets one `Block` object, the same every block, and each input becomes a JS value the first time the
node reads it in a block:

- **an events or bytes input** (`messages(port)`) is a reused `Message[]` of `{ frame, data, flags }`. The payloads
  are copied into one JS-owned buffer per port (grown, never shrunk), since plan memory may be freed after a swap,
  and a message's `data` view is made again only when its place in that buffer moves;
- **a control input or a param** (`control(id)`) is a reused `{ start, changes }`;
- **an audio port** (`audio(port)`) is `Float32Array` views straight over the plan's buffers, made again when a buffer
  or the block's length moves (so a ragged host costs about two objects per channel per block there), and detached
  before what they look at can be freed.

What a block hands out is good for that call only. **Outputs** go out through `send` and `emit`, which write the
plan's queue or control stream for the port directly, with no intermediate JS array. Ports are found by id through
atoms made when the instance, or the layout it reshapes to, is bound, in a linear walk (a layout has a handful of
ports), so a warm block allocates nothing native. Measured, a node written with indexed loops allocates nothing in JS
either, and one written with `for ... of` makes 7 allocations (360 bytes) a block
([ScriptNodes.test.cpp](../packages/native/test/engine-graph/ScriptNodes.test.cpp)).

**The block's transport** (frames, sample rate, tempo, ppq at block start, playing) comes from `rp_process`. The
Engine builds it from the fields it built the old `DspBlockInfo` from, so the kernel sees the same numbers.

### 2.4 Reshape

Before B3a an instance's layout was fixed for its life: a settings change that would alter it was a rebuild
(`rp_node_type::layout_for`'s contract). The kernel cannot work that way. Its ports are per system, and its
state must survive a system being added: `setSystems` keeps every surviving id's tick counter and role
scratch, and every project stage's state (the Launchpad session), and prunes only removed ids. A rebuild
cannot carry that state by copying it either, since the new instance is created on the control thread while
the old one is still advancing on the audio thread.

So, while ABI v1 is unshipped, `prepare_settings` gained a fourth result, **`RP_PREPARE_RESHAPE`**: keep this
instance, with the layout `layout_for` gives for the new settings.

- The planner asks `prepare_settings` on **every** settings change, whether or not the layout moved: only the
  instance knows whether it can keep up with a new layout. `RP_PREPARE_SWAP` for a changed layout is a
  `node-contract` error, and `RP_PREPARE_RESHAPE` with the layout unchanged is a swap.
- A reshape keeps the instance (its node id and type are unchanged) and binds the new plan's ports to it **by
  stable port id**. What is bound to a layout lives in a per-layout `PortState`, which each plan holds
  ([PlanStorage.hpp](../packages/native/src/graph/PlanStorage.hpp)): the layout, the param, control-output and
  resource-output stores, and the control side's records (the document values sent, the wired params, the last
  mask). A reshape builds a new one on the control thread while the running plan still uses the old, sharing into it,
  never copying, each store whose port or param persists: a param whose id, type, range and enum labels match (any
  other starts at its default), a control or resource output whose id, kind and resource type match.
- Feedback wires keep their last block, as they already do across a plan swap when a wire's key (its two
  endpoints) and shape are unchanged ([Planner.cpp](../packages/native/src/graph/Planner.cpp) `front`); a queue
  front whose source's capacity changed starts empty.
- The prepared settings commit **at the swap, on the block thread**, through the existing settings-commit path,
  in push order with every other command, so the first block of the new plan runs with them. A reshape that changes
  the layout always brings a `ports_changed`, after its `commit_settings`, so the node has the settings the mask
  belongs to. A script node receives the settings in a JS `onSettings(settings)` hook.
- A node that cannot reshape returns `RP_PREPARE_REBUILD`, as before. A C++ node opts in with `static constexpr bool
  reshapes`. A script type whose definition says `reshapes: true` answers `RP_PREPARE_RESHAPE` for every change its
  definition accepts; one without answers `RP_PREPARE_SWAP` while the layout stays the one it was created with and
  `RP_PREPARE_REBUILD` once it moves.

**The commit wait.** `setGraph` waited, up to its adoption timeout (2 s), for every published settings commit to be
adopted, because a C++ node's prepare may read its current settings and must not race the audio thread's commit. B1
never produced a commit; in B3a every structure edit carries one to the kernel. So the wait now applies only to a
commit whose node reads its current settings to prepare. A type promises the opposite with
`RP_TYPE_STATELESS_PREPARE` on `rp_node_type.flags`, a plan records whether any commit it carries is to a type
without it (`PlanStorage::awaitsAdoption`), and `GraphHost::waitForCommits` waits only for such plans
([GraphHost.cpp](../packages/native/src/graph/GraphHost.cpp)). Every script type is stateless (the control-side
runtime checks the new settings alone, and the planner already knows whether the layout moved); a C++ node says so
with `static constexpr bool stateless_prepare`, which a `static_assert` refuses beside `needs_rebuild` (that reads the
current settings). Consecutive kernel commits then queue on the ring and apply in push order (§10 says what that
bounds).

### 2.5 The bundle, embedded

The script-node bundle ([bundle.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/script/bundle.ts), whose one production type is the
kernel node) is esbuilt to a global-code IIFE and compiled to QuickJS bytecode at build time with the in-tree `tjsc`,
without `-m`, as the render worker is: the target `retroplug-script-bundle`
([bundles.cmake](../packages/native/cmake/bundles.cmake)), a derived C array under `build/native/` compiled into
`retroplug-backend` and never committed. Each Engine loads it into both runtimes at construction and registers the
script node types it defines; `Engine(sampleRate, chunks)` loads another bundle instead, which is how the native tests
run their toy nodes (the test-only twin, `retroplug-script-test-bundle`). Every host therefore has the same node types
with no boot call, and the boot-time `dsp.loadKernel(dsp.compileScript(__DSP_KERNEL_BUNDLE__))` in
`pluginControlPlane.ts` and `bootSession.ts` is gone. If the bundle fails to load, no script type is registered, so
every document naming one is refused (`unknown-type`), and the Engine logs why.

The bundle is 658 KB and still carries zod (about 567 KB of it) through the kernel node's settings schema and
`dspRoles.ts`; B3b removes it. Both runtimes load it, which costs memory and construction time, not per-block time:
making a script host and loading the bundle into it takes about 11 ms in a Release build.

### 2.6 Queue capacity

A plan queue holds 256 messages and 4 KB unless its port says otherwise (`kDefaultQueueMessages` /
`kDefaultQueueBytes`), and drops what does not fit. The old staging vectors were unbounded, so a large SysEx or a
burst of tracker sync bytes that passed them would be dropped on a wire. So an events or bytes port's descriptor may
declare its capacity, `"capacity": { "messages": n, "bytes": n }`, either part or both, each at most 1 Mi messages
or 16 MiB (in C++ `rp::bytes_out::sized<rp::capacity{...}>`, in TS `events.out(capacity)`). A wire carries its
**source's** queue, and a feedback wire's front is sized from the source too, so only output capacities bound
anything: `rp.host.midi-in`'s and `rp.host.controller-in`'s (§3.3), every kernel output (§4.1) and the Game Boy's
`serialOut` (§3.2), which also sizes the MI.OUT feedback front and so stays fixed. Inputs, the system nodes' inputs and
`rp.host.midi-out` need none.

Queues are allocated per plan, two plans' worth during a swap, and B3a replans on every structure edit, so the large
capacities stay modest: tens of KiB, not the cap. An output with no wire writes one shared scratch queue of the
default size. Control streams keep 64 changes a block, and the overwrite a full one makes is not counted. Drops are
counted: the executor folds each block's `dropped` into the producing instance's count and the host's
(`GraphHost::droppedMessages()`, and `droppedMessages(id)` for one node), `reclaim` names a node the first time it
drops, and `Engine::droppedMessages` reaches TS through the harness facet (`audio.droppedMessages()`). The parity rig
fails any render that dropped a message.

## 3. Ports and host I/O

### 3.1 System node inputs

Every system node gains four inputs, mapped onto core calls `SystemBase` already has (so no `dynamic_cast`;
[SystemNodes.cpp](../packages/native/src/host/graph/SystemNodes.cpp)):

| Port | Kind | Core call |
|---|---|---|
| `serialIn` | bytes | `pushSerialIn(frame, byte)`, one call per byte |
| `midi` | events | `onMidi`, with the old rule: a message longer than a `MidiEvent`'s inline data goes down `pushCoreBytes`, unframed |
| `bytes` | bytes | `pushCoreBytes(frame, data, size, flush)`, the flush flag riding `RP_MESSAGE_FLUSH` |
| `buttons` | events | `pressButton(button, down)`, a 2-byte payload `[button, down]` |

A node applies them once, at the top of its `prepare`, where `process` starts too, so a linked Game Boy's coupled
group (which steps through `rp.step/1` and never calls `process`) has them all before any member steps. They go in
the old fan-out's order, `serialIn`, then `midi`, then `bytes`, then `buttons`, each in queue order. Only MIDI before
bytes is observable, on the NES, where both land in the same FIFO: a flushed bytes message drops what the FIFO still
holds, the same block's MIDI included, as it did. A Game Boy's `midi` input has no effect, as before (SameBoy's
`onMidi` queues into a list nothing reads); mGB and LSDj hear MIDI through `serialIn`.

### 3.2 The Game Boy's `serialOut`

The Game Boy node has a `serialOut` output (bytes): the bytes its core captured on the serial port this block while
MI.OUT capture is armed (the build-time `serialOutCapture` flag, or `setSerialOutCapture`). It replaces the engine's
per-block gather into `pendingSerialOut_`. That gather dropped the bytes' frames, and the kernel read them without
any; the port carries each byte at frame 0, so the kernel reads exactly what it read before. The node copies the
core's log in `finish`, only while the port is connected, and the core clears it at its next `prepareForBlock`.

Capture clocks a bit every sample frame while the Game Boy holds an external-clock transfer (SC = 0x80), so an armed
port carries about one byte every 8 frames, idle bytes included, not only MI.OUT data. Its capacity, 4096 messages and
4096 bytes, therefore covers blocks up to 32768 frames, while `setMaxBlockFrames` allows 65536: accepted for B3a, and
noted. It is fixed, so the feedback wire from it keeps its front across every plan swap (§2.6).

### 3.3 Host I/O nodes

| Node | Ports | Replaces |
|---|---|---|
| `rp.host.midi-in` | out `midi` (events; 2048 messages, 64 KiB) | `pendingMidi_` handed to the kernel |
| `rp.host.midi-out` | in `midi` (events) | `DspRuntime::midiOut_`; feeds `Engine::midiOut()` |
| `rp.host.controller-in` | out `midi` (events; 1024 messages, 16 KiB), out `connected` (control) | `pendingControllerMidi_` and the per-block `controllerConnected` flag |
| `rp.host.controller-out` | in `midi` (events) | `DspRuntime::controllerOut_`; feeds `Engine::controllerOut()` |

They are the package `rp.host.io` ([HostIoNodes.hpp](../packages/native/src/host/graph/HostIoNodes.hpp)), each over
the engine's `rp.engine.host-io/1` service, without which none activates. The engine keeps staging what the hosts
hand it (`stageMidi`, `stageControllerMidi`, the controller-connected state): the plugin and the SDL host stage on
the audio thread, the harness and the CLI through the command ring, as before. Each staging is a flat arena, every
message's frame and place in one byte buffer, reserved at construction for what its input node carries in a block,
so staging allocates nothing until a block stages more. The input nodes take what is staged at the top of their
block; what no node takes, in a plan with no input node, is dropped at the block's end rather than carried. The
output nodes append to the buffers the plugin, the SDL host and `drainMidiOut` read, which the engine clears at the
top of each block.

`controllerConnected` is a control value. `rp.host.controller-in` writes a change at frame 0 on the block the flag
flips, since a node cannot set an output's start (the start is the last block's end), so a reader takes the start and
any change at frame 0: `startValue` in [defineNode.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/graph/defineNode.ts). That value is
the old per-block flag.

### 3.4 Frame order

ABI queues are frame-ordered: Phase A's `pushMessage` clamps a message whose frame is earlier than the last one
up to it. Host MIDI is not always staged in frame order. The plugin stages the DAW's MIDI events first
([PluginDSP.cpp](../packages/native/plugin/PluginDSP.cpp), `stageMidi(e.frame, ...)`) and then each moved
automation slot's CC at frame 0, so a block can stage `[100, 300, 0]`. Before B3a the NES FIFO and the SMS sync role
stable-sorted by frame, so that CC landed at frame 0, while SameBoy's serial queue, which releases only the byte at
its front, took it after the frame-300 byte.

`rp.host.midi-in` **stable-sorts** the staged MIDI by frame (an insertion sort, in place, without allocating) before
it pushes:

- the NES and SMS get exactly what they got (a stable sort of what they stable-sort);
- a Game Boy now receives a frame-0 automation CC at block start, before the block's notes. That is a
  **deliberate behaviour change**: frame 0 is when the automation happens, and a host that splits blocks at
  automation points (FL Studio) already puts it there. Parity cannot see it (`renderBlocks` refuses unsorted
  MIDI), so it has its own tests (§7.2).

The kernel's own output needs no sort. It sends out of frame order in two places, both LSDj sync modes: the
Arduinoboy protocol (a row byte at its note's frame, then START / STOP and the clocks at frame 0) and MI.MAP (a row
byte or the 0xFE note-off at its note's frame, then the 0xFF clocks at frame 0; §10). Both go only to SameBoy's
front-release serial queue, where the clamp raises the late bytes to the row byte's frame and the core takes them in
the same order as before. The kernel node pushes each sink call in emission order, and the plan delivers it to the
core in that order.

### 3.5 The N8 cart mirror

The merge ported the cart mirror as native logic in `runKernelStage`: for the first NES in slot order, its
core-MIDI and core-bytes went to the host's core-byte sink (`N8Link`) before the core's dispatch. B3a makes it
`rp.n8.cart-mirror`, a native node in the package `rp.n8` with inputs `midi` and `bytes`, which `buildGraph` wires
from the **first NES's** kernel `sys-<id>.midi` and `sys-<id>.bytes` outputs (an output fans out to any number of
inputs for free). It calls the sink for every MIDI message, then every byte message (the old order, flush flag
included), skipping an empty one, and does nothing while no sink is set. Its settings, `{ "system": <id> }`, name the
system it mirrors and change nothing it does, so its prepare is stateless. `Engine::setGraph` refuses (`cart-mirror`)
a second mirror and one naming a system not in the slots, and records the one it names with the plan:
`Engine::cartMirrorSystemId` reads the running plan's, for the hosts' "is a cart mirrored" test (no raw DAW MIDI to
the cart while one is) and for the `stageSystemMidi` mirror. `Engine::cartSystemId`'s walk is gone.

The two small items the merge left are done: the comments that cited a "BlipToaster host LFO" consuming CC76-79 now
name the routing and risa's sync, and `EngineCartMirror.test.cpp` judges a message staged at the cart against the
plan adopted ahead of it in the same drain.

## 4. The kernel node

### 4.1 Settings and ports

`rp.dsp.kernel` is a TS node ([kernelNode.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/script/kernelNode.ts)), defined with
`defineNode` in the script-node bundle around the unchanged `DspKernel`, with a registry of the DSP roles alone. Its
settings are the kernel's `KernelStructure` plus one fact per system:

```ts
{ project: RoleInstance[], systems: { id: number, pipeline: RoleInstance[], serialOut: boolean }[] }
```

`serialOut` is true for a Game Boy, the one system that has the port. `project` and `systems` default to empty, so a
document that names the type with no settings plans as an empty kernel; a role's `config` defaults to `{}` (its `kind`
and a system's `id` are required), and the ids are integers from 1 to 2^32 - 1 and must be distinct, which the old
kernel did not check (§10). Its ports, from those settings:

| Direction | Ports |
|---|---|
| in | `midiIn` (events), `controllerIn` (events), `controllerConnected` (control), `sys-<id>.serialOut` (bytes) for each system with `serialOut` |
| out | `sys-<id>.serialIn`, `sys-<id>.midi`, `sys-<id>.bytes`, `sys-<id>.buttons` for each system; `midiOut` (events); `controllerOut` (events) |

Ports are named by system id, never position, so a reshape (§2.4) binds a surviving system's ports to the
same wires. The outputs' capacities come from what the whole `test:native` suite sends through them in one block,
measured with the fixtures (parity included, 2.2 million kernel blocks up to 8192 frames): each has room for 16 times
that or more, messages and bytes, but for the two byte sizes noted:

| Output | Messages | Bytes |
|---|---|---|
| `sys-<id>.serialIn` | 1024 | 1 KiB |
| `sys-<id>.midi` | 512 | 64 KiB, `rp.host.midi-in`'s, so a SysEx the host stages whole reaches the system whole |
| `sys-<id>.bytes` | 256 | 1 KiB |
| `sys-<id>.buttons` | 64 | 128 |
| `midiOut` | 1024 | 8 KiB, a decoded MI.OUT stream at its densest |
| `controllerOut` | 256 | 4 KiB |

At 16 bytes a message plus its bytes, that is about 95 KiB of queues per system per plan, with 32 KiB more for the
kernel's own two outputs and 96 KiB for `rp.host.midi-in`'s.

### 4.2 Per block

`process` builds the same `BlockInput` `DspRuntime::processBlock` built, afresh each block: the block info from the
transport, `controllerConnected` (only when true, read with `startValue`, §3.3), `midiIn` from its port, `serialOut`
by concatenating each system's `sys-<id>.serialOut` input in the order the settings list the systems (slot order, as
`buildGraph` writes them), the still-unfed `buttons` / `keys` as empty arrays, and `controllerIn` from its port when a
surface sent something. It calls `DspKernel.processBlock` with a `SinkTarget` whose methods push into the output
ports: `pushSerialIn` one byte per message on `sys-<id>.serialIn`, `emitCoreMidi` on `sys-<id>.midi`, `pushCoreBytes`
on `sys-<id>.bytes` (flush as the flag), `pressButton` on `sys-<id>.buttons` at frame 0, `emitMidiOut` on `midiOut`
(§4.4), `emitControllerOut` on `controllerOut` at frame 0. A sink call for an id with no ports (an unknown id) is
dropped, as the old fan-out skipped an id it could not find.

### 4.3 Structure changes

`onSettings(settings)` calls `setSystems(settings)`, so a structure change keeps the old rules exactly:
surviving ids keep their tick counter and role scratch, removed ids are pruned, project stage state survives.
Every structure change is a reshape (the definition says `reshapes: true`), so the kernel's instance is never
rebuilt.

### 4.4 Host MIDI out

`drainMidiOut` reports which system emitted each message, and its emission order matters: a project stage (the
Launchpad controller addressing a real Game Boy) emits before every system stage. Per-system output ports would
lose that order. So `midiOut` is one port in emission order, and each message's payload is prefixed with the
emitting system's id (4 bytes, little-endian). Only `rp.host.midi-out` reads that port; it strips the prefix
into `Engine::midiOut()`'s `system` field, and skips a message too short to hold one. The prefix is private to B3a: in
B3b each protocol node has its own `midiOut` port and `rp.host.midi-out` takes the id from its wiring.

### 4.5 A throw

Before B3a a JS exception in `processBlock` was dropped: the sink calls made before it stood, and the next block
called `processBlock` again. The kernel node keeps that rule: the script host catches the throw, keeps what was
pushed, counts it on the block thread (`Engine::scriptThrows`), keeps the first one's text in a fixed 512-byte buffer
for `reclaim` to log once on the control thread, and runs the next block. It does not return `RP_FAULT`, whose latch
would turn a transient error into MIDI that stays dead until a rebuild. B3b's protocol nodes may opt into the latch:
a definition with `faultOnThrow: true` faults on a throw, and a `process` that returns `"fault"` faults too.

## 5. The TS side

### 5.1 `buildGraph`

The model gains each system's `pipeline` and the project's stages; `kernelProjection` still computes them from
the store (B3b moves that logic into `buildGraph` itself). The document
([buildGraph.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/graph/buildGraph.ts)) gains:

- `rp.host.midi-in`, `rp.host.controller-in`, `rp.host.midi-out`, `rp.host.controller-out`;
- the kernel node (`kernel`) with its settings (§4.1), the systems in slot order (positional MIDI routing reads it),
  and its wires: `midi-in.midi -> kernel.midiIn`, the controller pair, each `kernel.sys-<id>.*` output to
  `sys-<id>`'s input of the same name, each Game Boy's `sys-<id>.serialOut -> kernel.sys-<id>.serialOut` as a
  **feedback** wire (MI.OUT's one block of latency), `kernel.midiOut -> midi-out.midi`,
  `kernel.controllerOut -> controller-out.midi`;
- `rp.n8.cart-mirror` (`cart`) wired from the first NES in slot order, when there is one.

The kernel runs before the systems because its wires say so, not because it is listed first. The 840 goldens changed
on purpose and were re-recorded from `buildGraph` (every model gains an empty structure; the audio part of every
document is unchanged); the native goldens test keeps planning and running every one of them, with the embedded
kernel. B2's remark that two slot orders can build one document no longer holds, since the kernel lists its systems
in slot order; `EngineGraph`'s dedupe key keeps the slots all the same.

### 5.2 The stores

`ProjectStore.publishGraph` runs `projectKernelStructure` (with the controller projection, which moved in from
`appHost`) and publishes the systems with their pipelines, the routing and the project stages as one model,
`EngineGraph.publish({ systems, routing, project })`. A system's pipeline carries only the roles that have a DSP
behaviour (`SystemsStore.graphSystems`), so a model, palette or asset edit leaves the document as it was. An edit to a
role the kernel runs (an LSDj mode change), a MIDI-routing change, a controller edit and a polled song or start-edge
change publish, like any structural edit; `EngineGraph`'s dedupe drops a publish that changes nothing. A project load
that throws places what it adopted with their pipelines. `syncDspFromStore`, its push and the kernel half of the
`onSystemsChange` wiring are gone; the hook stays for the structure's other observers, the UI and the plugin's
watched ROMs.

### 5.3 `DirectGraph`

`DirectGraph` gains `setPipeline(id, roles)` and `setProjectStages(stages)`, each a publish without a tap re-arm
([directGraph.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/graph/directGraph.ts)). A system it adds or replaces starts with no
pipeline, and until `setProjectStages` there are no project stages, so no MIDI is routed to any system; a refused edit
puts the structure back. The callers moved mechanically, as B2 moved the build calls: 20 direct `test-native` files
moved their 32 `dsp.setSystems` pushes onto `setPipeline` / `setProjectStages`, 30 store-built ones dropped the
kernel load and the sync hook, and `render.ts` (the CLI `render` and the UI's `RenderHost`) and the two NES export
sessions dropped their manual sync, since the stores they build through now publish the pipelines themselves. The
harness's `stageMidiIn(bytes, frame?)` takes a frame (the RPC refuses one past `renderAudio`'s 1024-frame block), and
`MockBackend.kernelSettings()` reads the kernel's settings out of a published document.

### 5.4 What went

The `dspSetSystems`, `dspLoadKernel` and `compileScript` RPCs (the facets' union went from 90 methods to 87);
`DspRuntime` whole (the kernel's context, its sinks and thunks), `dspRuntime.ts`, `dspKernelBundle.ts` and
`__DSP_KERNEL_BUNDLE__`; the CLI session's `dsp` client and its SDK declaration; native's `KernelNode` and
`rp.engine.kernel/1`, `runKernelStage` and its fan-out, `Engine::loadKernel` / `setSystems`, the `SetSystems` and
`LoadKernel` commands, `pendingSerialOut_` and its gather, both `Engine::cartSystemId` overloads, and
`SystemTable`'s transitional host-MIDI flags (the engine now drops unclaimed staging at the end of every block).

What stayed: `ScriptCompiler` (the native tests compile toy nodes with it), `DspCommand`, the `Dsp*` profiling structs
(now in `ScriptHost.hpp`, which TS mirrors), `DspKernel.setSystems` in TS until B3b, and the `dsp*` profiling and
trace RPC names `dsp-bench`, `nes-bench` and `tools/run-profile.sh` use. The script host took over the runtime's
profiling: a profile build's allocation window per Engine block, auto-GC pinning, a timed collection, and the trace
window, in which every script node's `process` is a `dsp-kernel` span (spec/08 has the detail).

## 6. Block size

The engine takes any block from 1 to 8192 frames, and a frame stamp is an offset inside its block, so a host
that splits a block (FL Studio splits at automation and tempo points, down to 1 frame) is giving it two blocks.
Three properties are worth stating:

- **Frame 0 is the block's start.** Under splitting hosts it is exactly when automation happens, which is what
  the sort at the source (§3.4) relies on.
- **MI.OUT's latency is one block, not a fixed time.** In samples it is the previous block's length, so it
  varies with a splitting host. That was true before B3a, and the feedback wire keeps it bit for bit.
- **A script node costs one JS call per block.** Measured (§7.4): about 0.08 us with nothing to pass and 0.17 us with
  a message in and out, flat in node count and block size, against a 1-frame block's 22.7 us at 44.1 kHz. B3b's
  protocol nodes multiply calls by node count, so a 1-frame block means several JS calls per sample, and that is
  affordable: the main design's "batch consecutive script nodes into one call, not built until measured"
  ([§4.9](modular-graph-design.md)) is measured and not needed (§9).

Parity rendered the same scenes in 64, 199, 512, 1024 and 8192-frame blocks, a mixed cycle, and an edge segment with
a 7-frame block, but never a 1-frame block or a ragged FL-style split, until B3a's first commit recorded both (§7.1).

## 7. Testing

### 7.1 Parity, extended first

Before any B3a code existed, four parity groups were recorded on the merged engine (fa05b121), in three splits:
`1` (1-frame blocks), `fl` (the repeating ragged list `[33, 1, 222, 1, 7, 4096, 2]`) and `fl256` (a 256-frame buffer
split inside at automation points, `[256, 33, 1, 222, 255, 1, 1, 255, 7, 249]`), with MIDI, automation CCs and
transport points on block edges, on the first and last frame of a block and in 1-frame blocks
([blocks-tiny.ts](../packages/retroplug/test-native/parity/blocks-tiny.ts)):

- `blocks-tiny-mgb` and `blocks-tiny-nes` (mGB and BlipToaster at 44.1 and 48 kHz, fixture-free, so CI runs them);
- `blocks-tiny-lsdj` (LSDj MIDI sync, Arduinoboy, MI.OUT and master sync) and `blocks-tiny-risa` (risa host sync),
  both fixture-only.

The Arduinoboy cases also show that defect ([B0 design §2.5](modular-graph-phase-b0-design.md)) is not "every block
carries a tick": it stays silent in `1` and `fl256` and plays in `fl`, where six blocks of seven carry none. LSDj
master sync was recorded in the same splits, at 44.1 and 48 kHz, with its defect pinned (41357271, B0's eighth): in
small blocks its decoder reads a stopped LSDj's idle flood as clocks (§10). The pinned cases are
`masterSync-44100-{1,fl,fl256}`, which play and stop, and `masterSync-48000-{1,fl,fl256}`, silent (B0's sixth defect),
so their messages are the flood alone.

Segments are short, since 1-frame blocks multiply the block count. B3a is held to strict parity: every
group, with the fixtures present and `RP_FAIL_ON_SKIP=1`, and every commit of B3a held it bit for bit.

### 7.2 The deliberate change

Catch2 cases ([HostIo.test.cpp](../packages/native/test/engine-graph/HostIo.test.cpp)) hold `rp.host.midi-in`'s sort
(frame order, ties in staging order, nothing allocated, from staging to the queue). `parity/host-midi-order` stages
plugin-style MIDI (notes, then a frame-0 CC) through `stageMidiIn` on mGB and on BlipToaster: each renders exactly what
the same messages staged in frame order render, and the Game Boy differs from the CC placed after the notes, its old
behaviour. `nes-core-bytes` sends a 60 KiB SysEx and requires it to reach the NES FIFO whole, with no drop.

### 7.3 Reshape and the script host

- Native tests with a toy reshaping node (`retroplug-graph-test`): the instance is kept, its ports are rebound by id,
  a feedback wire keeps its last block, the settings commit at the swap, a node that returns `RP_PREPARE_REBUILD` is
  rebuilt.
- Toy TS nodes ([ScriptNodes.test.cpp](../packages/native/test/engine-graph/ScriptNodes.test.cpp)): input and output
  marshalling, sends past capacity refused and counted, layouts from the control-side runtime, a reshaping node kept
  and a non-reshaping one swapped or rebuilt, creation at adoption and release at reclaim on the block thread, a
  throw's count and the latch, the warm block path allocating nothing native; ThreadSanitizer runs a plan's script
  nodes on an audio thread while the control thread plans, reshapes, rebuilds and reclaims them.
- The kernel node ([KernelNode.test.cpp](../packages/native/test/engine-graph/KernelNode.test.cpp)), in a plan with the
  host I/O nodes: host MIDI under every routing, every LSDj sync mode, risa and smsggdj host sync, a controller
  session, state across structure changes (survivors go on, a removed id is pruned), a throw, and a reshape under a
  running audio thread. Each case is held to digests of everything the node sent, recorded while the old kernel
  stage still ran beside it, block by block, and was found equal to it.

### 7.4 The bench

[ScriptBench.test.cpp](../packages/native/test/engine-graph/ScriptBench.test.cpp), hidden from the normal run
(`build/bin/retroplug-engine-graph-test "[bench]"`), Release, 44.1 kHz on a Ryzen 9 9950X, medians of 7 runs. It ran
while both kernels existed (9217a026), so it timed the kernel node against the old kernel stage over the same blocks.

**A script node's call.** Chains of 1, 4, 16 and 64 pass-through TS nodes (`rp.bench.pass`, indexed loops) between a
native source and sink: about 0.08 us a node with nothing to pass (0.35% of a 1-frame block) and 0.17 us with one
message in and out, flat in node count and block size, with no JS or native allocation per block. 64 nodes take
5.4 us, 24% of a 1-frame block, which has room for about 280 calls with nothing to pass, or 130 passing a message.

**The kernel node against the old kernel stage**, over mGB, an LSDj in MIDI sync and a NES on `nes-n8-midi`,
`sendToAll`, playing at 120 bpm, a host message every 441 frames and each Game Boy's MI.OUT at its maximum, a byte
every 8 frames; no core on either side:

| Block | Old kernel stage | Kernel node | Ratio | JS allocations a block |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 frame | 1.95 us | 2.59 us | 1.33 | 25 |
| 64 frames | 5.0 us | 7.9 us | 1.57 | 81 |
| 512 frames | 24.2 us | 38.8 us | 1.61 | 431 |

The JS allocations are the same on both sides, and the plan's native nodes take 0.03 to 0.16 us of the node's time. The
gap is per message: the `Message` arrays refilled, then the kernel's own `BlockInput` copy of them, and one send per
output. Idle MI.OUT bytes dominate the larger blocks on both paths: at 512 frames the 128 the two Game Boys send cost
about 21 us on the old stage and 35 us on the node (about three JS allocations a byte), and with the bytes left out a
local run measured 1.87 against 2.46 us, 2.09 against 2.85 and 2.99 against 4.33. Capture is armed only for an LSDj
in a MIDI-out mode, so the table is the worst case. The numbers decide B3b's granularity (§9).

### 7.5 Acceptance

Strict parity (all 29 files, the new groups among them, 197 cases); `pnpm test`, `test:native`, `test:plugin`,
`test:ui`, `test:node`, `typecheck`, `check:docs`; the thread and address sanitizers; the Reaper checks
(including the LSDj sync and MI.OUT renders and the editor checks); `sdl:smoke` and `sdl:pipewire`; the
BlipToaster and NESVJ consumer suites against the built CLI.

## 8. How it lands

As B2 did: a working prototype built and verified on a scratch branch first, a plan written from it, then
executed task by task with review. In order, as built:

1. The new parity groups, recorded on the merged engine (fa05b121), and master sync's tiny-block defect pinned in
   them (41357271).
2. Reshape: the ABI result, the planner's keep-and-rebind, the settings commit, the stateless-prepare flag (9f6fc91d).
3. Port capacities in descriptors, and drops reaching the host (ac6cda2d).
4. System node inputs, the Game Boy's `serialOut`, the host I/O nodes and `rp.n8.cart-mirror`, beside the old path
   (5c015d22).
5. The script host: the two runtimes, the shim, marshalling, the embedded bundle, the ABI's type context (2a1f730b).
6. The kernel TS node (15f56ebb), then the flip: `buildGraph`'s wiring, the stores publishing the structure,
   `DirectGraph`'s calls and their callers moved (6595a6a7).
7. The bench (9217a026). It compares the kernel node with the kernel stage it replaces, so it moved ahead of the
   deletion, while both existed.
8. Delete the fan-out, the RPCs and the native kernel node, after moving the runtime's profiling onto the script host
   (b9287877, 37cc4b80).
9. The docs.
10. The acceptance run.

## 9. Left for B3b

The bench (§7.4) settles how B3b is cut: one node per role is affordable at 1-frame blocks, and batching is not
needed.

- **One protocol node per role** (`mgb.midi`, `lsdj.sync`, `risa.sync`, `sms.sync`, `n8.midi-to-fifo`, MIDI routing,
  the Launchpad controller), each with its own ports; the kernel node and `DspKernel` deleted. Split per role, the
  bench's structure (four roles) makes three more script calls a block, about 0.25 to 0.5 us, 1 to 2% of a 1-frame
  block.
- **No batching** of consecutive script nodes into one call: the main design's §4.9 "not built until measured" is
  measured and not needed. It would matter only at hundreds of script nodes on 1-frame blocks, the Reaktor-scale case
  (1000 empty nodes take about 80 us a block).
- **Write protocol nodes as `rp.bench.pass` is written**: indexed loops over the `Message` views, nothing allocated
  per block. A node's cost is what its JS does, not the call.
- **Wire a Game Boy's `serialOut` only into a node that decodes MI.OUT**, so a Game Boy without one pays nothing for
  an armed capture's idle bytes.
- `kernelProjection`'s special cases (the synthesized `midi-routing` and Launchpad stages, the forced
  `lsdj-sync` mode for MI.MAP) moved into `buildGraph`.
- A per-product script-node bundle with no zod in it.
- How several stages' outputs merge into one system input: each core must still get all its MIDI before all its
  bytes (the NES FIFO, §3.1), and `rp.core.merge`'s output is default-sized, so merging the kernel's large wires needs
  a merge whose output capacity its settings give.
- The `apu-render` span starts where the last script node's `process` ended, which is right while every script node
  runs before the systems, as in B3a; a protocol node placed after a system would need it revisited.

Before B3b starts, the LSDj master-sync fix lands on its own (§10).

## 10. Found while building

- **A commit made the next edit wait, and then the ring bounded edits.** `GraphHost::setGraph` waited up to its
  2 s adoption timeout for every published settings commit, because a C++ node's `prepare_settings` may read its
  current settings and must not race the audio thread's commit. B1 never produced a commit, so the wait never ran; in
  B3a every structure edit carries one to the kernel. With audio running that costs at most a block, but a host that
  stops calling `process` while the plugin stays active (DPF's CLAP `stop_processing` does nothing) would have frozen
  the UI 2 s per edit and then refused it `busy`. The wait now applies only to commits to a type without
  `RP_TYPE_STATELESS_PREPARE` (§2.4). So consecutive kernel commits queue on the 256-slot command ring instead, and
  while no block runs (a burst of edits, or that CLAP host) every queued plan holds its buffers until it is adopted, and
  past 256 `setGraph` answers `busy`. That was kept for B3a: it is bounded, and a refused edit is resent, since
  `EngineGraph` keeps the model it was asked for and sends the next document even when it matches (B2's refusal
  contract). Coalescing queued, unadopted plans is the alternative, should it bite.
- **The ABI's type-level calls had no context.** `descriptor`, `layout_for`, `query_memory` and `create` received
  no hint of the type they were called through, so one host could not serve several types through one set of
  functions, which is what the script host's one type per definition needs. They now take the `rp_node_type` first,
  and it gains a trailing `ctx`, null for a C++ node (§2.2).
- **`SystemNode::finish` wrote silence into every connected output** through its audio view, whatever the port's
  kind. Nothing but audio outputs was ever connected until the Game Boy's `serialOut`, whose queue it would have
  overwritten; it now silences audio outputs only.
- **An unbounded MI.OUT gather.** With the old kernel loaded but the kernel node in its place, the engine went on
  gathering MI.OUT into `pendingSerialOut_`, which only the old kernel stage cleared, so it grew without bound once
  capture was armed. The flip deleted the gather in the same change, and a plan with no `rp.host.midi-in` (or
  `controller-in`) now drops what was staged at the block's end rather than letting it grow.
- **LSDj master sync's stopped-LSDj detector depends on the block size.** `arduinoboyMasterSyncBlock`
  ([lsdjArduinoboy.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/lsdjArduinoboy.ts)) calls a block holding more than 16 serial-out
  bytes (`MASTER_SYNC_IDLE_FLOOD`) the stopped LSDj's idle flood. A stopped LSDj sends a few thousand bytes a second,
  so no block of fewer than about 150 frames at 44.1 kHz ever holds 16, and the handshake decodes as clocks: 10497
  MIDI messages in 1-frame blocks against 101 in 1024-frame ones; and at a fast tempo an 8192-frame block can pass 16
  while LSDj plays and read as stopped. It is pinned as it is (§7.1). By the user's decision it is fixed right after
  B3a, before B3b ports the decoder, as its own change re-recording exactly the cases it moves (`lsdj-modes`'
  `masterSync-44100` and `masterSync-48000` may move too, since the same threshold decides their boot noise). The fix
  needs a window across blocks, trading spurious clocks at the stop edge against a few milliseconds of clock latency.
- **The NES path cannot see one block of delay at 1-frame blocks.** BlipToaster's output does not change when every
  event of the edge segment moves by one frame (a lone note-on moved by a frame changes it about once every 67 frames
  at 48 kHz), and in 1-frame blocks a frame is exactly one block of latency, so `blocks-tiny-nes`' `1` cases are blind
  to it. Its ragged splits, whose blocks are mostly far longer than a frame, pin it; mGB hears a one-frame move in
  every split.
- **MI.MAP sends out of frame order too.** §3.4 as designed named only the Arduinoboy protocol; MI.MAP also sends a row
  byte at its note's frame and then its 0xFF clocks at frame 0. Both reach only SameBoy's front-release serial queue,
  so a frame-ordered queue's clamp changes nothing the core sees: the equivalence test applied the clamp to the old
  stage's output, counted the frames it raised, and parity held bit for bit.
- **Duplicate ids are refused.** The old kernel took a structure naming one system id twice without a word; the kernel
  node's settings refuse it ("two systems have the same id"), as they refuse an id outside 1 to 2^32 - 1.
- **The bench's numbers** (§7.4): a script call costs about 0.08 to 0.17 us whatever the node count or block size,
  the kernel node 1.3 to 1.6 times the old kernel stage, the gap per message, and idle MI.OUT bytes most of all. One
  node per role is affordable; batching is not needed (§9).
- **Staging is allocation-free.** Host and control-surface MIDI are staged into a flat arena each (every message's
  frame and place in one byte buffer), reserved at construction for what the input node carries, and two
  no-allocation cases hold it, from a direct `stageMidi` and through the command ring. The output side still
  allocates: `rp.host.midi-out` and `controller-out` append one vector per message to the engine's buffers, the next
  candidate.
- **The TS stripper does not build outside the repo.** `retroplug-ts-stripper-bundle` fails in a build directory
  outside the source tree: [build-ts-stripper.mjs](../tools/build-ts-stripper.mjs) sets no `absWorkingDir`, unlike
  `build-ui.js`, so esbuild resolves its `typescript-5` alias against the build's working directory. Pre-existing, and
  worth a fix of its own.
````

+**How an instance takes new settings.** The planner asks `prepare_settings` on every settings change, whether or not
+the layout moved, and it answers one of four results: **swap** (`RP_PREPARE_SWAP`: the layout is unchanged, and the
+prepared object commits at the plan swap), **reshape** (`RP_PREPARE_RESHAPE`: keep this instance with the layout
+`layout_for` gives the new settings; the planner rebinds its ports by id, carries over by id what its params and
+control outputs hold, and commits at the swap, §5.3), **rebuild** (`RP_PREPARE_REBUILD`: a fresh instance, a new ROM
+say) or **invalid**. A swap for a changed layout is a `node-contract` error, and a reshape that leaves the layout as
+it was is a swap. A reshape that changes the layout always brings a `ports_changed`, after its `commit_settings`, so
+the node has the settings the mask belongs to.
+
+**What a commit holds back.** Unless a type declares `RP_TYPE_STATELESS_PREPARE` in `rp_node_type.flags`, the host
+never calls its `prepare_settings` while a `commit_settings` for the same node may still be in flight, so the node
+may read its current settings there to compare against; `setGraph` waits for such a commit to be adopted first
+(§5.3). A type that declares the flag promises its prepare reads nothing a commit writes, so its commits never
+make `setGraph` wait. Every script type declares it ([B3a §2.4](modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md)); a C++ node does
+with `static constexpr bool stateless_prepare`, which rules out `needs_rebuild`.
+
 **Ports and params are resolved per instance**, because a `+`'s input count or a mixer's width depend on
 its settings. The type descriptor shows the defaults (for documentation and future UIs). Everything is
 addressed by **stable string ids** in documents and saved state; the planner maps ids to indices for the

+**Per-node call overhead.** One JS call per TS node per block replaces the kernel's single `processBlock`
+call. Measured in B3a ([B3a §7.4](modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md), a Release build at 44.1 kHz, where a 1-frame
+block has 22.7 us): a script node's call costs about 0.08 us with nothing to pass and 0.17 us with one message in and
+out, marshalling included, flat in node count and block size, with nothing allocated per block for a node written
+with indexed loops. One node per role is therefore affordable even at 1-frame blocks, and batching consecutive
+script nodes into one call is not needed: it would matter only at hundreds of script nodes on 1-frame blocks (1,000
+empty nodes take about 80 us a block), which is the Reaktor-scale case to revisit then. What a node costs beyond
+that is what its own JS does.

+once blocks run again.

+### Host I/O, the system nodes' inputs and queue capacities
+
+The kernel's input and output are wires the planner sees
+([modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md](../docs/modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md) section 3). The host
+I/O nodes ([HostIoNodes.hpp](../packages/native/src/host/graph/HostIoNodes.hpp)) reach the engine
+through its host service `rp.engine.host-io/1`
+([HostServices.hpp](../packages/native/src/host/graph/HostServices.hpp)) and do not activate without
+it:
+
+| Node | Ports | Does |
+|---|---|---|
+| `rp.host.midi-in` | out `midi` (events: 2048 messages, 64 KiB) | takes the staged host MIDI, stable-sorted by frame in place (an insertion sort: the plugin stages a block's DAW events in order, then each moved automation slot's CC at frame 0) |
+| `rp.host.midi-out` | in `midi` | each message is the emitting system's id, 4 bytes little-endian, then the MIDI; it lands in `Engine::midiOut` tagged with that system (a message shorter than the prefix is dropped) |
+| `rp.host.controller-in` | out `midi` (events: 1024 messages, 16 KiB), out `connected` (control) | takes the staged control-surface traffic, all at frame 0; `connected` is 1 while a surface is attached, from frame 0 of the block (a change at frame 0 on the block the flag flips, since a control output's start is the last block's end) |
+| `rp.host.controller-out` | in `midi` | appends each message to `Engine::controllerOut` |
+| `rp.n8.cart-mirror` | in `midi` (events), in `bytes` | settings `{"system": <id>}`; hands the core-byte sink every MIDI message, then every byte message with its flush flag, in queue order, skipping empty ones; nothing while no sink is set |
+
+`Engine::setGraph` refuses (`cart-mirror`) a document with a second cart mirror, or one whose `system`
+is not one of the slots. The system it names goes into the plan's `SystemTable`, and
+`Engine::cartMirrorSystemId()` reads it off the running plan: while it is non-zero the plugin and the
+SDL standalone stop forwarding raw DAW MIDI to the cart (it would arrive twice, the second copy
+unrouted), and a `StageSystemMidi` aimed at that system reaches the cart too. The node's settings
+change nothing it does, so it prepares statelessly and a change is a swap.
+
+Every system node has four inputs, mapped onto core calls `SystemBase` already has. It applies them
+at the top of its `prepare` (where `process` starts too, and which a linked group runs for every member
+before any of them steps), each in queue order, the inputs in this order:
+
+| Input | Kind | Core call |
+|---|---|---|
+| `serialIn` | bytes | `pushSerialIn(frame, byte)`, one call per byte |
+| `midi` | events | `onMidi`; a message longer than a `MidiEvent` holds goes down `pushCoreBytes`, unframed |
+| `bytes` | bytes | `pushCoreBytes(frame, data, size, flush)`, the flush flag riding `RP_MESSAGE_FLUSH` (and each message handed to the sync trace) |
+| `buttons` | events | `pressButton(button, down)`, from a 2-byte payload `[button, down]` |
+
+The order shows only on the NES, where MIDI and bytes land in the same FIFO: a flushed byte message
+discards the MIDI queued ahead of it. A Game Boy's `midi` input has no effect (SameBoy's `onMidi`
+queues into a list nothing reads); mGB and LSDj hear MIDI through `serialIn`. The Game Boy also has a
+`serialOut` output (bytes): after `finishBlock`, while it is connected, the node copies the bytes its
+core captured on the serial port this block, each a message at frame 0 (the core clears its log at
+its next `prepareForBlock`). Capture runs only while armed (the build-time `serialOutCapture` flag, or
+`setSerialOutCapture`; TS arms it for LSDj's two MIDI-out modes), and then takes a byte every 8 frames
+while the Game Boy holds the port for an external clock, idle bytes included. The port's capacity is
+fixed at 4096 messages and 4096 bytes, which covers blocks up to 32768 frames, so the feedback wire to
+the kernel keeps its front across every swap.
+
+An events or bytes port may declare its queue's capacity (`rp::bytes_out::sized<rp::capacity{...}>` in
+C++, `events.out(capacity)` / `bytes.out(capacity)` in TS), by default 256 messages and 4096 bytes, at
+most 1 Mi messages and 16 MiB. A wire carries its source's queue, so only an output's capacity bounds
+anything: the host inputs above, the Game Boy's `serialOut`, and each of the kernel's outputs
+([kernelNode.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/script/kernelNode.ts): per system `serialIn` 1024 messages /
+1 KiB, `midi` 512 / 64 KiB, `bytes` 256 / 1 KiB, `buttons` 64 / 128 B; `midiOut` 1024 / 8 KiB,
+`controllerOut` 256 / 4 KiB), each sized from what the suites send through it in one block, with
+margin. Queues are allocated per plan, and an unwired output writes a shared scratch queue of the
+default size. A push that does not fit is dropped and counted on its queue; after each block the
+executor adds the counts to the producing instance's atomic and the GraphHost's, `GraphHost::reclaim`
+names a node the first time its outputs drop, and `Engine::droppedMessages()` (the harness RPC
+`droppedMessages`) reads the total, which the parity rig and the suites hold at zero.
+

+- **The block.** A node's `process` gets one `Block` object, the same every block: `messages(port)` a
+  reused array whose payloads are copied into one JS-owned buffer per port, `control(id)` a reused
+  `{ start, changes }`, `audio(port)` `Float32Array` views straight over the plan's channel buffers
+  (made again only when a buffer or the block length moves, and detached before what they look at can
+  be freed), and `send` / `emit` writing the plan's output queues directly, a send past a queue's
+  capacity refused and counted. Ports are found through atoms made when the instance or its new layout
+  is bound, so a warm block allocates nothing native, and a node written with indexed loops nothing in
+  JS either. So **a `JSValue` never crosses out**. The **drift-exact PPQ tick clock lives entirely in
+  the JS kernel** (`walkTicks`); native passes only the block's transport in.
+- **A throw** in `process` is caught and counted, the block's output up to it stands, and the node runs
+  again next block; a definition that says `faultOnThrow`, or a `process` that returns `"fault"`,
+  faults instead (bypassed from then on). Throws in `create`, `onSettings`, `portsChanged` and
+  `activate` are counted too (`Engine::scriptThrows()`); the first one's text is kept on the block
+  thread in a fixed buffer and logged once by `reclaim`.
+
+Every entry into a runtime re-anchors with `JS_UpdateStackTop` because the driving thread differs
+(the control thread on the pull path, the audio thread while running), and QuickJS's stack-overflow
+guard is calibrated against the thread that last entered it. A profile build profiles the audio
+runtime there ([08-profiling.md](08-profiling.md)).

+
+[`buildGraph`](../packages/retroplug/src/graph/buildGraph.ts) is a pure function from the model
+(`{ systems, routing, project, shape }`) to the document `setGraph` plans
+([modular-graph-phase-b2-design.md](../docs/modular-graph-phase-b2-design.md) section 2.1; the node
+order, the routing as wiring and the host shapes are in [02-native-host.md](02-native-host.md)).
+Besides the system nodes and their mixing it places the DSP kernel between the host's I/O and the
+systems ([modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md](../docs/modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md) section 5.1):

+- `midi-in` (`rp.host.midi-in`) and `controller-in` (`rp.host.controller-in`), wired to the kernel's
+  `midiIn`, `controllerIn` and `controllerConnected`;
+- `kernel` (`rp.dsp.kernel`), its settings the structure: `{ project, systems: { id, pipeline,
+  serialOut }[] }`, the systems in slot order, `serialOut` true for a Game Boy;
+- each `kernel.sys-<id>.serialIn` / `.midi` / `.bytes` / `.buttons` wired to that system node's input
+  of the same name, and each Game Boy's `sys-<id>.serialOut` back to `kernel.sys-<id>.serialOut` as a
+  feedback wire, so MI.OUT reaches the kernel a block after the core sent it;
+- `cart` (`rp.n8.cart-mirror`, settings `{ system }`), wired from the kernel's `midi` and `bytes`
+  outputs for the first NES in slot order, when there is one;
+- `midi-out` (`rp.host.midi-out`) and `controller-out` (`rp.host.controller-out`), fed from the
+  kernel's `midiOut` and `controllerOut`.
+
+[`EngineGraph`](../packages/retroplug/src/engineGraph.ts) is one control-plane context's publisher:
+`publish({ systems, routing, project }, { rearmTap })` makes that its model, builds the document at
+its host shape and sends it, skipping the send when the document's canonical text and slots match the
+last one that planned, so an edit that changes nothing sends nothing (a re-arm is sent all the same,
+and after a refusal the next document is sent even if unchanged).
+[`DirectGraph`](../packages/retroplug/src/graph/directGraph.ts) is the publisher for callers with no
+stores (the native tests, the CLI's analysis sessions and the offset tools; one per process,
+`directGraph()`). Its `add` / `replace` / `remove` keep its systems list in slot order (add
+appends, replace keeps the slot, remove shifts later slots down), a system it adds or replaces has an
+empty pipeline, and the kernel's structure is two calls of its own, each a publish:
+`setPipeline(id, roles)` and `setProjectStages(stages)`. Until `setProjectStages` names a
+`midi-routing` stage, no host MIDI is routed to any system.

 ## Running as a script node
 
 The kernel runs as the script node `rp.dsp.kernel`
 ([kernelNode.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/script/kernelNode.ts), docs/modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md
-section 4) inside the script host's **bare QuickJS audio context** (no txiki) on the audio thread,
-distinct from the control-plane runtime; see [01-architecture.md](01-architecture.md) for the
-two-runtimes model and [02-native-host.md](02-native-host.md) for the script host.
-
-**The bundle** ([script/bundle.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/script/bundle.ts)) is esbuilt to one
-IIFE, compiled to bytecode at build time and embedded in every native binary, so every Engine has the
-kernel node with no boot call. The node builds its **own** registry (**`dspRoles` only**: no core
-roles, no ROM providers).
-
-**Its settings** are the kernel's structure (`KernelStructure`, plus whether each system has a
-`serialOut`), and a structure change reshapes it: the instance is kept and `setSystems` keeps each
-surviving id's state. **Its ports** are per system, named by id: it reads `midiIn`, `controllerIn`,
-`controllerConnected` and each Game Boy's `serialOut` of last block, builds the kernel's `BlockInput`
-at the block-start ppq, and its `SinkTarget` sends each sink call on the addressed system's
-`serialIn` / `midi` / `bytes` / `buttons` output (wired to that system node's input of the same name),
-or on `midiOut` / `controllerOut` (to the host output nodes).
+section 4) inside the script host's **bare QuickJS audio context** (no txiki), on whichever thread runs
+blocks, distinct from the control-plane runtime; see [01-architecture.md](01-architecture.md) for the
+runtimes and [02-native-host.md](02-native-host.md) for the script host.
+
+**The bundle** ([script/bundle.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/script/bundle.ts)) holds the kernel
+node's definition, appended to the global `__rp_scriptNodes` by `registerScriptNodes`
+([script/register.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/script/register.ts)). It is esbuilt to one IIFE,
+compiled to QuickJS bytecode at build time and embedded in the backend library, and every Engine runs
+it in both of its script contexts at construction, so every host has the kernel node with no compile
+or load call. The node builds its **own** registry (**`dspRoles` only**: no core roles, no ROM
+providers), shared by every instance, since a behaviour keeps its state in the kernel's scratch bags.
+
+**Its settings** are the kernel's structure plus one fact per system:
+`{ project: RoleInstance[], systems: { id, pipeline: RoleInstance[], serialOut: boolean }[] }`. Every
+field but a system's `id` and a role's `kind` has a default (a document naming `rp.dsp.kernel` with no
+settings plans an empty kernel, and a role's `config` defaults to `{}`), and each id is an integer from 1 to 2^32 - 1,
+distinct from the others: two systems under one id are refused. `serialOut` is true for a Game Boy,
+the one system node with that output.
+
+**Its ports** follow from the settings and are named by system id, never position:
+
+| Direction | Ports |
+|---|---|
+| in | `midiIn` (events), `controllerIn` (events), `controllerConnected` (control), and `sys-<id>.serialOut` (bytes) for each system with `serialOut` |
+| out | `sys-<id>.serialIn` (bytes), `sys-<id>.midi` (events), `sys-<id>.bytes` (bytes) and `sys-<id>.buttons` (events) for each system; `midiOut` (events); `controllerOut` (events) |
+
+`buildGraph` wires them ([03-ts-layer.md](03-ts-layer.md)): the inputs from `rp.host.midi-in`,
+`rp.host.controller-in` and each Game Boy's `serialOut` (a feedback wire, so the kernel reads last
+block's MI.OUT), each `sys-<id>.*` output to that system node's input of the same name, and `midiOut`
+and `controllerOut` to the host's output nodes. Each output declares its queue's capacity, sized from
+the most the suites send through it in one block, with room to spare: `serialIn` 1024 messages / 1 KiB,
+`midi` 512 / 64 KiB (as many bytes as `rp.host.midi-in` carries, so a SysEx the host stages whole
+reaches the system whole), `bytes` 256 / 1 KiB, `buttons` 64 / 128 bytes, `midiOut` 1024 / 8 KiB,
+`controllerOut` 256 / 4 KiB. A send past one is dropped and counted (`Engine::droppedMessages`).
+
+**A structure change reshapes it.** The definition declares `reshapes`, so a settings change keeps
+the instance even when it changes the ports: the planner binds the new plan's ports to it by id (a
+surviving system's wires stay on its ports) and commits the settings at the plan swap, where
+`onSettings` hands them to `DspKernel.setSystems`. A surviving id keeps its clock and scratch, the
+project stages keep theirs, and a removed id is pruned ([Execution order](#execution-order)).
+
+**Each block** it builds the `BlockInput` afresh, field for field: the transport (`frames`,
+`sampleRate`, `tempo`, `ppqStart` at the block-start ppq, `transport`); `controllerConnected` when the
+control's value from frame 0 is non-zero (`startValue`: its start, or a change at frame 0, which is how
+`rp.host.controller-in` signals a flip); `midiIn`, and `controllerIn` when a surface sent something,
+copied from their ports as `{ frame, data }` with `data` a plain array (a role may keep one across
+blocks); each Game Boy's `serialOut` bytes, concatenated in the order the settings list the systems
+(slot order) and tagged with its id; and empty `buttons` and `keys` (no host feeds them yet). Its
+`SinkTarget` sends each sink call onto a port, in emission order:
+
+| Sink call | Port |
+|---|---|
+| `pushSerialIn(system, frame, byte)` | one byte at `frame` on `sys-<id>.serialIn` |
+| `emitCoreMidi(system, frame, data)` | `sys-<id>.midi` |
+| `pushCoreBytes(system, frame, data, flush)` | `sys-<id>.bytes`, the flush flag as `RP_MESSAGE_FLUSH` |
+| `pressButton(system, frame, button, down)` | `[button, down]` on `sys-<id>.buttons`, at frame 0 |
+| `emitMidiOut(system, frame, data)` | `midiOut`, behind the system's id as 4 little-endian bytes, which `rp.host.midi-out` strips into the message's system tag |
+| `emitControllerOut(data)` | `controllerOut`, at frame 0 |
+
+A call naming a system with no ports (an id not in the settings) is dropped. Host MIDI out is one port
+rather than one per system so that its emission order holds: a project stage (the Launchpad
+controller addressing a real Game Boy) emits before every system stage.
+
+**Frame order.** A queue is frame-ordered: a message pushed with an earlier frame than the one before
+it is raised to that frame. Two roles emit out of order onto a system's `serialIn`: Arduinoboy MIDI
+sync writes a row byte at its note's frame, then START / STOP and its clocks at frame 0, and MI.MAP
+writes row bytes at their note's frame, then its `0xFF` clocks at frame 0. Both drive only a Game
+Boy, whose serial queue begins a byte only once every byte ahead of it has gone, so raising a byte's
+frame to the one before it changes nothing the core sees.
+
+**A throw** in the kernel's JS is caught by the script host and counted (`Engine::scriptThrows`; the
+first one is logged): what the kernel sent before it stands, and the next block runs again.

+## 5. The node-graph engine: after B3a
+
+Phase B of [modular-graph-design.md](../docs/modular-graph-design.md) moves the engine onto the graph in
+steps, each held bit for bit to the parity baseline ([06-build-test.md](06-build-test.md)). B3a
+([modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md](../docs/modular-graph-phase-b3a-design.md)) is built: the kernel's
+input and output are real wires (host I/O nodes, `serialIn` / `midi` / `bytes` / `buttons` inputs on
+every system node, the Game Boy's `serialOut`, `rp.n8.cart-mirror`), the kernel runs unchanged as one TS
+node, `rp.dsp.kernel`, in the script host every Engine embeds, and the sealed native kernel node, its
+fan-out, the `dspSetSystems` / `dspLoadKernel` / `compileScript` RPCs and the boot-time kernel load are
+gone. Staged host MIDI is allocation-free (one flat arena per staging, reserved at construction). What is
+left, in order:
+
+- **The master-sync fix, before B3b.** The eighth recorded defect of design section 2.5 of
+  [modular-graph-phase-b0-design.md](../docs/modular-graph-phase-b0-design.md): LSDj master sync's decoder
+  ([lsdjArduinoboy.ts](../packages/retroplug/src/lsdjArduinoboy.ts), `arduinoboyMasterSyncBlock`) calls a
+  block carrying more than `MASTER_SYNC_IDLE_FLOOD` (16) serial-out bytes a stopped LSDj's idle flood, so
+  what it decodes depends on the host block's length: in small blocks a stopped LSDj's flood reads as
+  clocks, and a fast tempo in long blocks could pass 16 and read as stopped. The fix needs a window across
+  blocks, trading spurious clocks at the stop edge against a few milliseconds of clock latency. It is its
+  own change and re-records exactly the cases it moves (`blocks-tiny-lsdj`'s six `masterSync-*`, and
+  possibly `lsdj-modes`' `masterSync-44100` and `masterSync-48000`, whose boot noise the same threshold
+  decides), and it lands before B3b ports the decoder into a protocol node.
+- **B3b.** One protocol node per role (`mgb.midi`, `lsdj.sync`, `risa.sync`, `sms.sync`,
+  `n8.midi-to-fifo`, the MIDI routing, the Launchpad controller), each with its own ports;
+  `kernelProjection`'s special cases (the synthesized `midi-routing` and Launchpad stages, the forced
+  `lsdj-sync` mode for MI.MAP) moved into `buildGraph`; a script-node bundle with no zod in it (the
+  kernel's settings schema and `dspRoles.ts` carry it today); then the kernel node and `DspKernel`
+  deleted. How several stages' outputs merge into one system input is B3b's to decide; a system input

 | [10-multichannel-audio-out.md](10-multichannel-audio-out.md) | **Built** (steps 1–7; per-mapper NES expansion sub-channels remain). Outputting the individual console sound channels of one instance: Game Boy → 8 outputs (a stereo pair per channel, via a tracked SameBoy tap), NES → 5 mono stems or the hardware "stereo-mod" pins (via a `NesSoundMixer` edit). One mode-driven host seam (`channelLayout()` + a lane-counted `finishBlock`, with the graph TS builds wiring each stream to its lanes), the `channelSplit` / `pinSplit` / `stereoPinSplit` plugin options (menu rows `Channels` / `Pins` / `Stereo Pins`; a stereo stream takes a lane pair, a mono one a single lane, so the NES fits 8 outputs - except `Stereo Pins`, which spends a pair per pin so each is its own DAW track), and a `renderAudioPerChannel` CLI RPC feeding multichannel / per-stereo / per-mono WAV export. |
